title: Should, ought to, had better
goal: Give advice without sounding too strong
intro: Use “should” to give or ask for advice: “You should see a doctor.” “Ought to” means the same but sounds more formal. “Had better” is stronger: there is a warning in it. For softer advice, add “I think” or “maybe”.

rules.rule: had better (’d better) + base form: a warning.
examples: You’d better leave now or you’ll miss the train.

rules.rule: Soften it: I think you should… / Maybe you could…
examples: I think you should talk to her.
Maybe you could try again tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: You should to see a doctor.

mistakes.right: I don’t think you should worry.
mistakes.why: More natural: “I don’t think you should…”.

ex.q: You look tired. You ___ go to bed.
___ I bring anything to the party?
It’s going to rain. We ___ take an umbrella.
You should to apply for this job.
ex.fixed: You should apply for this job.

ex.q: What I should say to him?
ex.fixed: What should I say to him?

ex.q: I ___ think you should buy it. It’s too expensive.

ex.a: Maybe you should talk to your manager.

ex.q: Give advice with “should”: your friend has a headache.
ex.y: You should + base form, e.g. You should take a rest.

talk: A friend wants to improve their English quickly. Give them five pieces of advice using should, shouldn’t, and had better.
